title: Section 4 (Lines 36–50)
subtitle: The self-refilling wine, the goose chase, and the gods reveal themselves

words.p: adverb · Adverb of time, opening the new scene.
words.x: Bridges from the meal to the miracle — “while all this was going on…”.

words.p: adverb · Adverb of frequency, with haustum: “drained so many times”.
words.x: Stresses how often the bowl had been emptied — yet it keeps refilling.

words.p: participle · Perfect passive participle, accusative singular masculine, with crātēra: “(having been) drained”.
words.x: Part of the indirect statement after vident: they see the bowl, drained so often, refilled.

words.p: noun · Accusative singular (Greek, crātēra) — subject of the indirect statement after vident.
words.x: A Greek loan-word for the bowl in which wine was mixed with water. The Greek accusative ending -a adds epic colour.

words.p: verb · Present passive infinitive (replērī) in the indirect statement: “(that the bowl) was being refilled”.
words.x: Compound of re- (“again”) + pleō (“fill”). The passive hints that no human hand is doing the filling.

rows.en: Meanwhile they see the mixing bowl which had been drained so many times refilled

words.p: noun · Ablative singular, with suā: “of its own accord”.
words.x: Only the ablative sponte (and genitive spontis) survive; sponte suā is a fixed idiom.

words.p: adjective · Ablative singular feminine, agreeing with sponte: “of its own accord”.
words.x: Reflexive possessive — here referring to the wine itself.

words.p: preposition · Preposition governing sē: “by itself”.
words.x: per sē = “by itself” — restating sponte suā for emphasis (pleonasm).

words.p: pronoun · Accusative reflexive pronoun, governed by per: “by itself”.
words.x: Reflexive, referring back to the wine: it rises “through itself”, with no help.

words.p: conjunction · Enclitic conjunction, attached to per sē.
verb · 3rd person plural present indicative active (vident): “they see”.
words.x: A historic present: the present tense vividly dramatises a past event. It introduces the indirect statement.

words.m: grow up, increase, rise from below
words.p: verb · Present active infinitive (succrēscere) in the indirect statement with vīna: “(that) the wine was increasing”.
words.x: Compound of sub- (“up from below”) + crēscō (“grow”) — the wine level creeps upward.

words.p: noun · Accusative plural (vīna) — subject of succrēscere in the indirect statement.
words.x: The poetic plural vīna simply means “wine” (cf. English “waters”).

rows.en: of its own accord and the wine increasing by itself;

words.p: participle · Perfect passive participle used as adjective, nominative plural masculine, describing the couple: “astonished”.
words.x: Literally “struck by thunder” (tonitrus) — a pointed word, since Jupiter is the thunder god.

words.p: noun · Ablative singular — ablative of cause with attonitī: “astonished by the strangeness”.
words.x: From novus (“new”) — the never-before-seen marvel of the self-filling bowl.

words.p: verb · 3rd person plural present (pavent): “they are afraid”.
words.x: A vivid present — their fear is awe, not terror of harm.

words.p: noun · Ablative plural, with supīnīs: “with hands…”.
words.x: A 4th-declension feminine noun (cf. domus, anus).

words.p: conjunction · Enclitic conjunction, attached to manibus.
adjective · Ablative plural feminine, agreeing with manibus: “with upturned hands”.
words.x: manibus supīnīs describes the standard Roman posture of prayer, palms to the sky.

rows.en: Astonished by the strangeness, they fear with hands facing upwards,

words.p: verb · 3rd person plural present (concipiunt): “they form (prayers)”.
words.x: Compound of con- + capiō (“take”). With precēs: “they put together / utter prayers”.

words.p: noun · Nominative singular (Greek) — one of the subjects of concipiunt.
words.x: The old woman; her Greek name suits the Phrygian setting.

words.p: conjunction · Enclitic conjunction, attached to Baucis.
words.x: The pair -que… -que (“both… and”) links Baucis and Philemon — polysyndeton stressing their unity.

words.p: noun · Accusative plural — object of concipiunt.
words.x: Usually found in the plural; the singular is rare.

words.p: adjective · Nominative singular masculine, describing Philēmōn: “timid Philemon”.
words.x: Grammatically with Philemon, but it characterises both of the humble, awe-struck pair.

words.p: conjunction · Enclitic conjunction, attached to timidus.
noun · Nominative singular (Greek) — the second subject of concipiunt.
words.x: Baucis’s husband; the two are always named together.

rows.en: both Baucis and timid Philemon (begin) to form prayers

words.p: conjunction · Conjunction, joining concipiunt and ōrant.
noun · Accusative singular — object of ōrant: “they beg pardon”.
words.x: They apologise for the humble fare set before their (divine) guests.

words.p: noun · Dative singular (dapibus, here treated as plural form) — dative with venia: “pardon for the feast”.
words.x: A poetic word for a (ritual) meal. They ask forgiveness for so meagre a spread.

words.p: adjective · Dative plural, agreeing with parātibus: “for (their) non-existent preparations”.
words.x: Irregular: genitive nūllīus, dative nūllī. Here it stresses how unprepared they were.

words.p: conjunction · Enclitic conjunction, joining dapibus and parātibus.
noun · Dative plural, with nūllīs: “for the lack of preparations”.
words.x: From parō (“prepare”). They could offer no grand banquet to such guests.

words.p: verb · 3rd person plural present (ōrant): “they beg / pray”.
words.x: Related to ōs, ōris (“mouth”) — to plead aloud.

rows.en: and beg pardon for the feast and lack of preparations.

words.p: adjective · Nominative singular masculine, describing ānser: “a single goose”.
words.x: Stronger than ūnus — it underlines that this goose is their one and only possession.

words.p: noun · Nominative singular — subject of erat.
words.x: The couple’s sole livestock, soon to be hunted for the sacrifice.

words.p: verb · 3rd person singular imperfect (erat): “there was”.
words.x: Existential use: ūnicus ānser erat = “there was a single goose”.

words.p: adjective · Genitive singular feminine, with vīllae: “of the very small house”.
words.x: Superlative of parvus (“small”). It reinforces the couple’s poverty.

words.p: noun · Nominative singular, in apposition to ānser: “(the) guardian (of the house)”.
words.x: Geese were famous Roman watch-animals — they saved the Capitol from the Gauls by raising the alarm.

words.p: noun · Genitive singular, with minimae: “of the very small house”.
words.x: A grander word than casa, used here with gentle irony of their tiny home.

rows.en: There was (just) one goose, guardian of the very small house,

words.p: pronoun · Relative pronoun, accusative singular masculine (quem) — object of mactāre; antecedent ānser.
words.x: Connecting relative: “(and) this (goose), which…”.

words.p: noun · Dative plural (dīs, contracted) — dative of advantage with mactāre: “for the gods”.
words.x: dīs is a contracted form of deīs. The irony: the “gods” they mean to honour are the guests themselves.

words.p: noun · Dative plural (hospitibus), in apposition to dīs: “(for) the gods, their guests”.
words.x: hospes covers both “guest” and “host” — the ties of hospitality run both ways.

words.p: noun · Nominative plural — subject of parābant: “the owners”.
words.x: Here the couple, as owners of the goose and the house.

words.p: verb · Present active infinitive (mactāre) — complementary with parābant: “were preparing to kill”.
words.x: A technical word for ritual slaughter — they meant to make the goose a religious offering.

words.p: verb · 3rd person plural imperfect (parābant): “(they) were preparing”.
words.x: Imperfect tense — they were in the middle of trying, but never managed it.

rows.en: which the owners were preparing to kill for the gods, their guests;

words.p: pronoun · Nominative singular masculine (ille) — subject, referring to the goose: “it / that goose”.
words.x: Picks up the goose as a character in its own right for the chase.

words.p: adjective · Nominative singular masculine, describing ille (the goose): “swift”.
words.x: Set against tardōs (“slow”) of the couple — a pointed antithesis.

words.p: noun · Ablative singular — ablative of means / respect: “with its wing(s)”.
words.x: The goose’s speed comes from its wings; the elderly couple have no such advantage.

words.p: adjective · Accusative plural masculine (tardōs) — object of fatīgat, referring to the old couple: “the slow (pair)”.
words.x: The opposite of celer — the chase is comically one-sided.

words.p: noun · Ablative singular — ablative of cause/respect with tardōs: “slow because of (their) age”.
words.x: They are tardōs aetāte — slowed down by old age.

words.p: verb · 3rd person singular present (fatīgat): “(it) tires out”.
words.x: A historic present keeping the chase vivid — the goose exhausts the old couple.

rows.en: the goose, swift with its wings, wore them out as they were slow with age,

words.p: verb · 3rd person singular present (ēlūdit): “(it) eludes (them)”.
words.x: Compound of ex- + lūdō (“play, mock”) — the goose makes fools of them.

words.p: conjunction · Enclitic conjunction, joining fatīgat and ēlūdit.
adverb · Adverb of time, with ēlūdit: “eludes them for a long time”.
words.x: Stretches out the comic chase before the climactic tandem.

words.p: adverb · Adverb of time, marking the climax of the chase.
words.x: The decisive moment — at last the goose flees to the gods themselves.

words.p: conjunction · Enclitic conjunction, attached to tandem.
verb · est vīsus = 3rd person singular perfect passive of videō: “(it) seemed / appeared”.
words.x: est + the participle vīsus together form the perfect: “it seemed”.

words.p: participle · Perfect participle, nominative singular masculine (vīsus), with est: “it seemed (to have fled)”.
words.x: The passive of videō in the sense “seem”; it governs the infinitive cōnfūgisse.

words.p: preposition · Preposition governing deōs: “to the gods”.
words.x: Marks the destination of the goose’s flight.

words.p: pronoun · Accusative plural masculine (ipsōs), with deōs: “the gods themselves”.
words.x: Emphatic: the goose fled to the very gods — not just the disguised guests — revealing the truth.

rows.en: and eluded them for a long time and finally seemed to have fled for refuge

words.p: verb · Perfect active infinitive (cōnfūgisse) — in indirect statement after vīsus est: “(seemed) to have fled for refuge”.
words.x: Compound of con- + fugiō (“flee”) — to flee somewhere for protection.

words.p: noun · Accusative plural (deōs), governed by ad: “to the gods”.
words.x: The goose’s instinctive refuge with the gods exposes their divine identity.

words.p: noun · Nominative plural — subject of vetuēre: “the gods above”.
words.x: Literally “those above”, from superus (“upper”) — a standard poetic term for the gods.

words.p: verb · 3rd person plural perfect, vetuēre = vetuērunt (syncopated): “(they) forbade”.
words.x: Poets often shorten the perfect ending -ērunt to -ēre.

words.p: verb · Present passive infinitive (necārī) — after vetuēre: “forbade (it) to be killed”.
words.x: The gods spare the goose, sparing the couple a needless loss.

rows.en: to the gods themselves. The gods forbade it to be killed

words.p: noun · Nominative plural (dī, contracted) — predicate of sumus: “we are gods”.
words.x: dī is a contracted nominative plural of deus. The terse two-word revelation.

words.p: conjunction · Enclitic conjunction, joining the gods’ act to their speech.
verb · 1st person plural present (sumus): “we are”.
words.x: The momentous self-revelation: dī sumus — “we are gods”.

words.p: participle · Perfect passive participle, accusative plural feminine (meritās), with poenās: “deserved (penalties)”.
words.x: With poenās: “the punishment it deserves”.

words.p: conjunction · Enclitic conjunction, linking the two clauses of the gods’ speech.
verb · 3rd person singular future (luet): “(it) will pay”.
words.x: poenās luere is a stock idiom meaning “to pay the penalty”.

words.p: noun · Nominative singular — subject of luet: “the neighbourhood”.
words.x: A collective noun for the local people who refused the gods hospitality.

words.p: noun · Accusative plural (poenās) — object of luet: “(will pay) the penalties”.
words.x: Often plural in the idiom poenās luere / dare (“to pay the penalty”).

rows.en: and said 'We are gods, and the irreligious neighbourhood

words.p: adjective · Nominative singular feminine (impia), agreeing with vīcīnia: “the impious neighbourhood”.
words.x: Held over to the next line (enjambment) — the damning word lands with extra force. The opposite of the couple’s pietās.

words.p: verb · 3rd person plural perfect (dīxērunt): “(they) said”.
words.x: Frames the gods’ direct speech.

words.p: pronoun · Dative plural (vōbīs) — dative with dabitur: “it will be granted to you”.
words.x: Addressed to Baucis and Philemon — they alone will be spared.

words.p: adjective · Dative plural (immūnibus), agreeing with vōbīs: “to you, (being) exempt”.
words.x: From in- (“not”) + mūnus (“obligation, burden”) — free from the coming disaster.

words.p: pronoun · Genitive singular neuter (huius), with malī: “from this disaster”.
words.x: Points to the flood/destruction the gods are about to send.

rows.en: will pay the penalty it deserves; it will be granted to you to be exempt from this

words.p: verb · Present infinitive (esse) — subject of dabitur: “to be (exempt) will be granted”.
words.x: vōbīs immūnibus esse dabitur = “it will be granted to you to be exempt”.

words.p: noun · Genitive singular, with huius: “of this disaster”.
words.x: Here the coming destruction of the impious region.

words.p: verb · 3rd person singular future passive (dabitur): “it will be granted”.
words.x: Impersonal passive: “it will be granted (to you) to be exempt”.

words.p: adverb · Adverb, qualifying the commands that follow: “only / just (leave)”.
words.x: Introduces the single condition the gods set: just leave at once.

words.p: adjective · Accusative plural neuter (vestra), agreeing with tēcta: “your home”.
words.x: Possessive of vōs (“you”, plural) — the couple’s own dwelling.

words.p: verb · 2nd person plural present imperative (relinquite): “leave!”.
words.x: First of three commands (tricolon): leave… accompany… go.

words.p: noun · Accusative plural (tēcta) — object of relinquite: “(your) home”.
words.x: From tegō (“cover, roof”) — by metonymy, “roof” stands for the whole house.

words.p: conjunction · Conjunction, joining the commands.
words.x: A form of atque, used before consonants.

words.p: adjective · Accusative plural masculine (nostrōs), agreeing with gradūs: “our steps”.
words.x: Possessive of nōs (“we”) — the gods invite the couple to walk with them.

words.p: verb · 2nd person plural present imperative (comitāte): “accompany!”.
words.x: A deponent verb (passive form, active meaning). Second command of the tricolon. Related to comes (“companion”).

words.p: noun · Accusative plural (gradūs) — object of comitāte: “(our) steps”.
words.x: From gradior (“walk, step”) — “keep pace with us”.

words.p: conjunction · Conjunction, joining comitāte and īte.
preposition · Preposition governing ardua: “onto the heights”.
words.x: With the accusative it expresses motion towards — up the mountain.

words.p: adjective · Accusative plural neuter used as a noun (ardua), governed by in: “onto the steep heights”.
words.x: The neuter plural ardua means “the steep parts, the heights” — they must climb to safety.

words.p: noun · Genitive singular (montis), with ardua: “(the heights) of the mountain”.
words.x: The high ground will keep them safe from the flood to come.

rows.en: and accompany our steps and go together (with us) to the steep parts

words.p: verb · 2nd person plural present imperative (īte): “go!”.
words.x: An irregular verb. The third and final command of the tricolon.

words.p: adverb · Adverb, with īte: “go together”.
words.x: A tender close to the command — even the gods treat the couple as an inseparable pair.

notes.label: Historic Present
notes.body: Ovid switches to the present tense vident (“they see”) even though he is narrating past events. This historic present makes the action feel immediate and vivid — one moment the bowl is empty, the next it is full. The present tense captures that “wait, what?!” moment.
notes.exam: In an exam: “The historic present vident (‘they see’) creates immediacy, drawing the reader into the moment of discovery. Ovid makes us experience the miracle alongside Baucis and Philemon rather than hearing about it after the fact.”

notes.label: Pleonasm
notes.trans: of its own accord… by itself
notes.body: Ovid hammers home the miraculous nature here. Sponte suā means “of its own accord” and per sē means “by itself” — essentially the same thing said twice. This pleonasm (repetition for emphasis) stresses that nobody is topping up this wine. It is refilling itself.
notes.exam: In an exam: “The pleonasm sponte suā (‘of its own accord’) and per sē (‘by itself’) emphasises the supernatural nature of the miracle. Ovid’s redundancy is deliberate — he wants readers to grasp fully that this is happening without any human intervention.”

notes.label: Sibilance
notes.trans: of its own accord… by itself… to grow up
notes.body: Listen to all those “s” sounds: sponte suā… sē… succrēscere. This sibilance creates a hissing, whispering effect — almost like an incantation murmured under the breath. It is sound mimicking meaning: the wine is magically rising, and the language itself sounds magical.
notes.exam: In an exam: “The sibilance in sponte suā per sē-que… succrēscere creates an incantatory effect through the repeated ‘s’ sounds. This sonic quality reinforces the supernatural nature of the miracle — the language itself seems to whisper of magic.”

notes.label: Emotive Diction
notes.body: Attonitī literally means “thunderstruck” — struck by tonitrus (thunder). It is a strong word for shock, far beyond “surprised”. And here is the clever bit: they are being thunderstruck in the presence of Jupiter, the god of thunder. The couple have no idea why they feel this divine awe, but we do.
notes.exam: In an exam: “The participle attonitī (‘thunderstruck’) conveys the intensity of their shock at witnessing the miracle. The word literally means ‘struck by thunder’ (tonitrus), creating dramatic irony as they stand in the presence of Jupiter, the thunder god himself.”

notes.label: Ablative Phrase
notes.body: Manibus supīnīs literally means “with hands turned upward” — the standard Roman prayer posture, palms facing the sky to receive blessings from the gods above. Ovid uses this technical religious detail to show that Baucis and Philemon instinctively know how to behave: proper, pious, doing everything right.
notes.exam: In an exam: “The ablative phrase manibus supīnīs (‘with upturned hands’) describes the traditional Roman prayer gesture. This detail emphasises the couple’s instinctive piety — they respond to the miracle with proper religious reverence, not panic or greed.”

notes.label: Polysyndeton
notes.body: The couple are named together with the repeated -que (“both… and”), which is called polysyndeton. It emphasises their unity — they are a pair, a team, inseparable. The adjective timidus (“timid”) is sandwiched between them, and while it agrees grammatically with Philemon, it characterises them both.
notes.exam: In an exam: “The polysyndeton with -que… -que (‘both Baucis and… Philemon’) reinforces the couple’s unity. The interposed timidus (‘timid’) applies grammatically to Philemon but characterises them both, emphasising their humble piety.”

notes.label: Pathos
notes.body: This single goose (ūnicus) is all they have. It is not just a pet — it is described as the cūstōdia (“guardian”) of their tiny home (minimae vīllae). The pathos is thick: they are willing to sacrifice literally their only possession to honour their guests. That is next-level hospitality.
notes.exam: In an exam: “Ūnicus (‘only’) emphasises how precious the goose is — their sole possession. Calling it cūstōdia (‘guardian’) elevates its importance, while minimae vīllae (‘of the very small house’) reinforces their poverty. Their willingness to sacrifice it shows the depth of their pietas.”

notes.label: Dramatic Irony
notes.body: Dīs hospitibus means “for the gods, their guests” — but the couple do not know yet that their guests are gods. That is dramatic irony: we (the readers) know the truth, but they do not. They mean to sacrifice their goose “to honour the gods” by feeding the actual gods. It is both touching and darkly comic.
notes.exam: In an exam: “The phrase dīs hospitibus (‘for the gods, their guests’) creates dramatic irony. The couple intend to honour the gods by sacrificing their goose to feed their guests — unaware that their guests literally are gods. This irony heightens both the pathos and the humour of the scene.”

notes.label: Antithesis
notes.body: Picture the scene: the goose is celer (“swift”), zooming about on its wings (pennā), while the elderly couple are tardōs aetāte (“slow with age”), huffing and puffing to catch it. It is slapstick comedy — two old people chasing a goose round a tiny cottage — but with pathos too. The contrast of celer and tardōs is classic antithesis.
notes.exam: In an exam: “The antithesis between celer (‘swift’) and tardōs (‘slow’) creates both humour and pathos. The goose’s speed (pennā, ‘with its wings’) contrasts sharply with the couple’s age (aetāte), highlighting their vulnerability while adding a moment of comic relief.”

notes.label: Climax
notes.body: After all that chasing, we get tandem — “finally!” This little word marks the climax of the goose chase. And where does the goose flee? Ad ipsōs… deōs — “to the very gods themselves.” The emphatic ipsōs stresses that the goose fled to the actual gods, inadvertently blowing their cover.
notes.exam: In an exam: “Tandem (‘finally’) signals the climax of the scene. The phrase ad ipsōs… deōs (‘to the gods themselves’) is emphatic — ipsōs stresses that the goose fled to the very gods, not just their disguised human forms. This triggers the revelation.”

notes.label: Divine Revelation
notes.body: After ten lines of build-up — the miracle, the shock, the goose chase — the gods reveal themselves with just two words: dī sumus (“we are gods”). No fanfare, no dramatic monologue. The brevity is the point. Gods do not need to explain themselves; they state facts. The contrast with the frantic human activity beforehand makes this hit harder.
notes.exam: In an exam: “The revelation ‘dī sumus’ (‘we are gods’) is deliberately terse — just two words for this momentous declaration. The brevity creates impact, and the first-person plural (sumus) confirms their divine identity after the extended dramatic irony.”

notes.label: Enjambment
notes.body: Look where impia (“irreligious”) lands — pushed onto the next line, separated from the noun it describes (vīcīnia, “neighbourhood”). This enjambment makes you wait for the damning adjective: you read “the neighbourhood will pay the penalty it deserves…” and then BAM — “irreligious.” The delay adds weight to the condemnation.
notes.exam: In an exam: “The enjambment of impia (‘irreligious’) — pushed to line 47 and separated from vīcīnia (‘neighbourhood’) — creates a dramatic pause before the condemnation. This emphatic positioning highlights the moral contrast between the impious neighbours and the pious couple.”

notes.label: Tricolon
notes.body: The gods issue three commands in quick succession: “leave your home… accompany our steps… go together.” This tricolon — a group of three parallel imperatives — gives the speech a rhythmic, authoritative quality. Gods do not waffle; they give clear, clipped orders. The final simul (“together”) is touching: even in command, the gods recognise the couple as a unit.
notes.exam: In an exam: “The tricolon of imperatives relinquite… comitāte… īte (‘leave… accompany… go’) creates a commanding, authoritative rhythm appropriate to divine speech. The brevity contrasts with the couple’s humble prayers, and the final simul (‘together’) acknowledges their inseparable bond.”
